title: Mary in Carmel
hookLine: an order that calls Mary both mother and sister

cards: Families have their own names for the people they love: Mom, Nana, Auntie, Sis. The Carmelites carry Mary in their very name: they are the brothers and sisters of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel.
But inside the order, people speak of her in two ways that don't usually go together. She is their mother. And she is their sister.
One person, two names, two kinds of closeness. Today, Mary in Carmel.

teach.b: First, mother. At the cross, John's Gospel says, Jesus looks at his mother and at the disciple he loves, and gives them to each other. In the Douay-Rheims: "After that, he saith to the disciple: Behold thy mother."
Catholic tradition hears each disciple standing in that place.

Carmelites took it personally: the order has long called Mary its mother and patroness, and the brown scapular this path met earlier is worn as a sign of belonging to her. Second, sister. This is the surprising one.

A sister isn't above you; she's beside you, on the same road. Jesus says, in Matthew: "For whosoever shall do the will of my Father, that is in heaven, he is my brother, and my sister, and my mother."
Luke shows Mary doing that will, with her yes to the angel. So Carmelites see her as a fellow disciple, one of them, praying, listening, trusting in the dark. Third, the quiet one.

After the shepherds leave, Luke says: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." That's the Carmelite vocation in a sentence: not many words, a heart that keeps things and turns them over.
Teresa, John, Thérèse, Elizabeth all learned that kind of prayer, and Carmel sees Mary as the one who shows them how. Fourth, near, not distant.

Near the end of her life, Thérèse said Mary is more mother than queen: not a figure on a pedestal, but someone close enough to talk to plainly. Sister and mother: one who goes beside you, one who holds you.

how: Carmelites honor Mary as mother and sister: they keep her feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, some wear the brown scapular, and they greet her with the Hail Mary and with quiet, pondering prayer.

games.q: you're a new Carmelite novice. someone asks why you'd call the mother of God your sister. what do you answer?
o: because she walked the same road of faith, doing the Father's will.
because the title mother sounds too formal.
because sister is just a nickname with no meaning.
games.why: Jesus calls whoever does his Father's will his sister. Carmel sees Mary, who said yes to the angel, as a fellow disciple beside them.

practice: Greet Mary simply, the way you'd say hello to someone in the next room: no long prayer, no performance.
If you pray, use the angel's words from Luke, "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women," once, slowly, then stay quiet, the way Mary kept things in her heart.
If you don't pray, hold the picture of a young woman listening, and keep her company in the silence.

wordCard.voice: Mary in Carmel. The order's mother, who holds them, and their sister, who walks beside them in prayer. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: sister and mother. Carmel keeps both names for her, side by side. Rest well.
